tagline: Barrier islands and beach towns joined by a St. Johns ferry crossing.
intro: The A1A Ocean Islands Trail follows beaches and barrier islands for 39.7 miles through Nassau and Duval counties, with a ferry carrying the route across the St. Johns River. Florida Scenic Highways highlights its ecological variety, history and recreation; the state program designated the byway on July 26, 2016. Much of the road follows the seacoast, while in Jacksonville Beach A1A becomes the community’s main commercial corridor. The route links four small cities within the Jacksonville metropolitan area.

The ferry connection has its own history of public support. When state funding was vetoed for 2007–2008, Jacksonville assumed responsibility to keep the service from ending. Operation later passed to the port authority, and in March 2016 the Jacksonville Transportation Authority took permanent ownership and operation. The alternative road journey uses the Dames Point Bridge and runs 28 miles.

Begin in Fernandina Beach on Amelia Island, then follow A1A south across the Nassau River into Duval County. Amelia Island State Park brings together beaches, salt marshes and maritime forest beside this part of A1A. The ferry reaches Mayport’s commercial fishing village on the south bank; the road then turns east and south through Atlantic Beach, Neptune Beach and Jacksonville Beach to SR 202.

moments.title: American Beach
moments.text: American Beach offered Black vacationers a seaside resort when segregation denied them access to many public beaches. Abraham Lincoln Lewis and his Afro-American Life Insurance Company co-founded the community in 1935. The resort welcomed all visitors, though most were African Americans. Homes stood alongside hotels, restaurants and nightclubs. In 1977, Lewis’s granddaughter MaVynee Betsch returned to fight for its preservation. She planted trees on Lewis Street, gave history tours and raised awareness until her death in 2005. The historic district entered the National Register in 2002; a museum dedicated to A. L. Lewis opened in 2014.

moments.title: Fort George Island
moments.text: Oyster shells connect two different histories on Fort George Island. The Timucua village of Alicamani belonged to the Saturiwa chiefdom, and shell middens mark Indigenous occupation. Those middens contain discarded food remains as well as large quantities of shells. Later builders burned shells and mixed them into tabby concrete for the Kingsley plantation’s quarters for enslaved people and other island foundations. Zephaniah Kingsley was a slave trader as well as a planter. His main house, kitchen and barn have survived and been restored, and tabby quarters remain. The plantation site is part of the Timucuan Ecological and Historic Preserve.
moments.notice: Tabby concrete survives in the quarters built for enslaved people.

moments.title: Mayport Ferry
moments.text: A1A crosses the St. Johns aboard an automobile ferry between Fort George Island on the north bank and Mayport on the south. The crossing’s history reaches back to 1874, but service has had interruptions. After the port authority sold the backup vessel Blackbeard, the remaining Jean Ribault’s maintenance problems could suspend the service. In 2009, hull corrosion extended a routine dry-dock visit, leaving the crossing without service for a month. On the Mayport side, the United States Merchant Marine Memorial stands on the ferry grounds, where it was erected in 1999.
